The previous view had been a steady state view in which basically matter, the universe, everything was eternal and there had basically been unchanged since eternity. So it was a big challenge. Now I think there are lots of moves these days to try to monkey with the cosmology to get a bigger world, a multiverse, but basically that's a way of I think trying to get by the theistic implications of Big Bang cosmology. With regard to evolution, I don't know, I mean that's just a huge topic. I mean the continuity in the fossil record, I think there's a fair amount of common ancestry, but I'm certainly not an advocate of universal common ancestry. I just don't think the fossil record bears that out. I think the Cambrian explosion is a perfect example where you have just utter, you have these forms which are just there, proof, and there are no precursors. Then you might say, well, maybe fossilization just wasn't all that good and we missed it. But the thing is we can tell how good fossilization is by looking at extant organisms and seeing how well they're fossilized. And it turns out when you go to higher levels of classifications, families, orders, classes, actually fossilization percentages are very good. So they should be there. And we see also microorganisms, soft body plants in the pre-Cambrian rocks. So it seems to me that if you're going to try to push for common descent, you're not getting it from the full common descent, the monad to man evolution. I don't think the evidence supports that.
